items.stem: Evaluate Vrechopoulos et al.’s (2004) study of virtual store layouts, including a discussion of generalisability.
items.answer: Strength (controls): Using a virtual store meant products and prices were identical, so only the layout differed between conditions. Strength (usefulness): Online retailers can use the findings to design websites that are easy to use or that encourage browsing. Weakness (ecological validity): Shopping online in a simulated store is unlike walking through a real shop with crowds, sounds and smells. Weakness (generalisability): Participants were from one country and familiar with computers, so the findings may not apply to all shoppers. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which the physical environment of a store has a strong influence on what consumers buy. In your answer, you may refer to ecological validity and usefulness.
items.answer: Arguments for: North et al. (1999): French wine outsold German wine when French music played, and vice versa. Milliman (1982): slow-tempo music slowed shoppers and increased sales. Layout guides customers past more products. Arguments against: Effects are often small and depend on the type of shopper and product. Consumers may not be aware of the influence, but price, brand and need matter more. Field studies have little control over other variables. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Mateo compared the number of items sold per day from a display when slow-tempo or fast-tempo music was played in a store in Karachi. Table: Items sold per day — Slow-tempo music: 112, 97, 128, 103, 95, 133, 124, 109, 128, 108. Fast-tempo music: 78, 110, 97, 104, 93, 87, 106, 105, 87, 95. (a) Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here. (b) Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why. (c) Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study. (d) To what extent do these results support the prediction that shoppers on days with slow-tempo music will buy more items than shoppers on days with fast-tempo music? Use the data in your answer. (e) Explain why a repeated measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV. (b) No price promotions during the study. (c) Shoppers do not know they are in a study, so no personal data should be recorded. (d) Mean for slow-tempo music = 113.7 and fast-tempo music = 96.2; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 38 and 32) and the sample is small (n = 10 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (e) Repeated measures removes participant variables because the same people do both conditions, but order effects (practice or fatigue) and demand characteristics become more likely; counterbalancing would be needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2] (b) 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2] (c) 1 mark: ethical guideline named; 1 mark: applied to this study [2] (d) 1 mark: uses both means; 1 mark: judgement about direction; 1 mark: limitation such as overlap of scores, small sample or no statistical test [3] (e) 1 mark: advantage of the alternative design; 1 mark: problem it causes; 1 mark: applied to this study [3]

items.stem: Evaluate North et al.’s (1999) study of in-store music and wine sales in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about ethics.
items.answer: Strength (controls): Wines were matched on price and sweetness and the music alternated days, so the type of music was the main difference. Strength (ecological validity): It took place in a real supermarket with real shoppers buying with their own money. Weakness (sample of purchases): Relatively few bottles were sold in total, so a small number of shoppers could affect the pattern. Weakness (ethics): Shoppers did not consent and were influenced without awareness; only those who agreed answered the questionnaire. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of research on lighting in retail settings (for example Areni and Kim, 1994). Include at least one point about validity.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Retailers can use lighting cheaply to highlight products they want to sell. Strength (ecological validity): Studies in real stores measure real shopper behaviour, such as handling and buying products. Weakness (validity): Handling a product does not necessarily mean buying it, so effects on sales may be small. Weakness (controls): Field studies cannot control other influences such as time of day or type of customer. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.answer: (a) The slow-tempo music condition had a higher mean (104.5) than the fast-tempo music condition (83.7), suggesting that slow-tempo music increases sales. (b) Bar chart, because the IV has separate (discrete) categories, so the mean for each condition is shown as a separate bar with gaps between bars.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2] (b) 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: justification (discrete conditions / categories, not continuous data) [2]

items.stem: ‘The physical environment of a store has a strong influence on what consumers buy.’ To what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Arguments for: North et al. (1999): French wine outsold German wine when French music played, and vice versa. Milliman (1982): slow-tempo music slowed shoppers and increased sales. Layout guides customers past more products. Arguments against: Effects are often small and depend on the type of shopper and product. Consumers may not be aware of the influence, but price, brand and need matter more. Field studies have little control over other variables. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “A store layout in which a main path loops around the store, leading customers past all departments”?
items.answer: Racetrack layout
items.markingKey: Racetrack layout: a store layout in which a main path loops around the store, leading customers past all departments. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student writes: “A freeform layout makes it easiest to find a specific product quickly.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a grid layout for consumers.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Grid layouts are easiest for finding items; freeform layouts encourage browsing. (b) Advantage: products are easy to find and the layout is familiar, so shopping is quick. Disadvantage: it is repetitive and discourages browsing, and shoppers may have to walk long aisles.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength of Vrechopoulos et al.’s (2004) study of virtual store layouts in terms of controls.
items.answer: Using a virtual store meant products and prices were identical, so only the layout differed between conditions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to controls; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Tomás compared the number of items sold per day from a display when slow-tempo or fast-tempo music was played in a store in Bangkok. Table: Items sold per day — Slow-tempo music: 119, 107, 107, 118, 98, 96. Fast-tempo music: 108, 75, 87, 71, 87, 90. Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: Slow-tempo music: 107.5; fast-tempo music: 86.3.
items.markingKey: Slow-tempo music: 645 ÷ 6 = 107.5; fast-tempo music: 518 ÷ 6 = 86.3. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]

items.stem: A new bookshop is opening in Nairobi. The owner, Grace, wants customers to stay longer and buy more books on impulse. Recommend a store layout and explain your choice.
items.answer: A freeform layout, with displays of different shapes and themed tables, encourages browsing and impulse buying; or a racetrack that leads customers past all sections.
items.markingKey: 1 mark layout; 1 mark justification [2]

items.stem: A supermarket in Hanoi recorded daily sales (number of items from a promoted display) on 6 days with slow-tempo background music and 6 days with fast-tempo music. Table: Items sold per day — Slow-tempo music: 102, 95, 97, 91, 84, 110. Fast-tempo music: 81, 82, 94, 86, 81, 76. Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: The same days of the week in each condition, so that busy days are balanced.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: Ravi wants to find out whether the type of background music in a café affects how long customers stay. Design an observation to investigate this. Your plan must include: ethical issues, the type of observation and behavioural categories.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Structured observation with operationalised behavioural categories and time sampling; two observers to check inter-rater reliability; overt or covert as appropriate. Variables: IV: type of music; DV: time spent in the café (minutes). Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Singapore, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: “Vrechopoulos et al.’s (2004) study of virtual store layouts has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including controls in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Online retailers can use the findings to design websites that are easy to use or that encourage browsing. Strength (controls): Using a virtual store meant products and prices were identical, so only the layout differed between conditions. Weakness (ecological validity): Shopping online in a simulated store is unlike walking through a real shop with crowds, sounds and smells. Weakness (generalisability): Participants were from one country and familiar with computers, so the findings may not apply to all shoppers. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “When exposure to one stimulus makes related ideas more accessible and influences later behaviour”?
items.answer: Priming
items.markingKey: Priming: when exposure to one stimulus makes related ideas more accessible and influences later behaviour. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “North et al.’s study was a laboratory experiment.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe the procedure and findings of North et al. (1999).
items.answer: (a) Not correct. It was a field experiment in a real supermarket. (b) In a UK supermarket, French and German accordion music was played on alternate days next to a display of French and German wines of similar price and sweetness. French wine outsold German when French music played and German wine outsold French when German music played; few shoppers said the music affected them.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark procedure; 1 mark findings; 1 mark awareness [3]

items.stem: North et al.’s (1999) study of in-store music and wine sales can be evaluated in terms of sample of purchases. Explain one weakness of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: Relatively few bottles were sold in total, so a small number of shoppers could affect the pattern.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to sample of purchases; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A café owner in Madrid, Mohammed, wants customers to stay longer at lunchtime on quiet days but leave more quickly on busy days. Suggest how Mohammed could use music on busy days and explain why.
items.answer: Play faster music so customers eat more quickly and tables are freed for new customers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark fast music; 1 mark effect [2]

items.stem: A supermarket in Colombo recorded daily sales (number of items from a promoted display) on 7 days with slow-tempo background music and 7 days with fast-tempo music. Table: Items sold per day — Slow-tempo music: 106, 99, 102, 102, 96, 74, 102. Fast-tempo music: 98, 92, 73, 77, 91, 94, 94. (a) Calculate the range of scores for each condition. (b) The standard deviation for the slow-tempo music condition was 10.72 and for the fast-tempo music condition was 9.50. Explain what these values show.
items.answer: (a) Slow-tempo music: 32; fast-tempo music: 25. (b) The slow-tempo music condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent.
items.markingKey: (a) Slow-tempo music: 106 − 74 = 32; fast-tempo music: 98 − 73 = 25. 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2]

items.stem: ‘The physical environment of a store has a strong influence on what consumers buy.’ Discuss this view. In your answer, you may refer to usefulness and ethics of influencing consumers.

Layout guides customers past more products. Arguments against: Effects are often small and depend on the type of shopper and product. Consumers may not be aware of the influence, but price, brand and need matter more. Field studies have little control over other variables. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: What is meant by ‘crowding’?
items.answer: The subjective, unpleasant feeling that there are too many people in a space.
items.markingKey: Crowding: the subjective, unpleasant feeling that there are too many people in a space. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: With reference to research on lighting in retail settings (for example Areni and Kim, 1994), explain one strength relating to ecological validity.
items.answer: Studies in real stores measure real shopper behaviour, such as handling and buying products.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to ecological validity; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: With reference to research on lighting in retail settings (for example Areni and Kim, 1994), explain one weakness relating to validity.
items.answer: Handling a product does not necessarily mean buying it, so effects on sales may be small.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to validity; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A supermarket in Bangkok recorded daily sales (number of items from a promoted display) on 7 days with slow-tempo background music and 7 days with fast-tempo music. Table: Items sold per day — Slow-tempo music: 111, 99, 104, 95, 112, 103, 110. Fast-tempo music: 89, 100, 79, 88, 70, 108, 101. Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: Slow-tempo music: 104.9; fast-tempo music: 90.7.
items.markingKey: Slow-tempo music: 734 ÷ 7 = 104.9; fast-tempo music: 635 ÷ 7 = 90.7. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]

items.stem: A department store in Cairo is very busy at weekends. Managers notice that customers leave quickly without buying, and complain about being pushed in narrow aisles. (a) Use the concept of crowding to explain the customers’ behaviour. (b) Suggest two changes the managers could make.
items.answer: (a) High density and invasion of personal space create the unpleasant feeling of crowding, causing stress, so customers leave early. (b) Widen aisles or reduce displays; open more checkouts; manage entry numbers; use calm lighting and music.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark crowding; 1 mark consequence [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Manila is interested in how shoppers feel about crowded stores. Design an interview to test this. Your plan must include: one example question, ethical issues, how the data will be analysed and the type of interview. Then explain one weakness of your plan and how it could be overcome.
items.answer: Method: an interview. A structured or semi-structured interview with set questions asked in the same order; record and transcribe answers; train interviewers. Variables: topic: experiences of crowding; measure: rating scales and open answers. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Manila, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected. Weakness: for example a small or biased sample; overcome by a larger, more representative sample.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.
